title: Social Loafing
description: People exert less effort when working in a group than when working alone, relying on others to carry the load.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: People exert less effort when working in a group than when working alone, relying on others to carry the load.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: In a group project, one or two members do the bulk of the work while others coast.
A committee votes to “leave it to the chair.”
In a large meeting, many attendees never contribute but take credit for being present.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Silence during planning but criticism afterward.
Doing the bare minimum because “someone else will pick it up.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: The group is large, so individual effort feels invisible.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Social impact theory (Latané, 1981) says that as group size increases, personal responsibility diffuses and motivation drops, especially when individual output isn’t measured. Meta-analyses confirm the effect is robust across tasks.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: If you’re leading, assign specific tasks to specific people with clear deadlines.
If you’re a team member and see loafing, gently call it out: “I’d love to hear your input on this section.”

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming loafers are lazy by nature; often they are unconsciously reacting to structure.
Letting resentment build silently instead of addressing it early.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A marketing team of eight brainstorms a campaign. No one is assigned ownership. Three people throw out ideas; the rest nod. The final product is mediocre. The next time, the manager assigns each person one component with their name attached. Suddenly, all eight deliver.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: If you want everyone to row, make sure everyone knows the boat moves only when they pull their own oar.
